opening.title: Reports change for two different reasons
keyPoints: Meaning: count or warning classification.
Presentation: plain text or brackets.
Negative counts remain invalid in either format.
opening.narration: Our inspection tool must present the same count on two screens. One wants count equals six; another wants count colon six inside brackets. The tool also needs a warning report that chooses high above five and normal otherwise. We now have two reasons for change: what the report means and how the text looks. Begin by stating those reasons separately. A punctuation change should not force us to rethink the warning boundary, and a policy change should not force us to edit every format. The program builds strings in memory; its Writer name does not mean that it writes a file or contacts a service.
actions: Create a two-by-two table of report meaning and output format.
opening.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Two useful reports, two useful formats

question.prompt: What two choices form the four report combinations?
question.answer: Count versus warning report, and plain versus bracket formatting.

opening.title: One report needs only one function
keyPoints: Validate the count.
Build one clear result string.
Do not split a dimension that does not vary yet.
opening.narration: This first program serves exactly one requirement: render a valid count in the plain format. A single function makes the contract visible and keeps the implementation short. The function returns a string value, so the caller owns the returned characters. It throws before formatting a negative number because negativity is a report-domain error. There is no need yet for an abstract Writer or a family of Report classes. We will earn that separation by showing independent changes, rather than adding it in anticipation of every possible future request. Notice that a valid zero is accepted; absence of work is still a meaningful count.
actions: Explain why the negative test belongs before formatting.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch07.json → Two useful reports, two useful formats

question.prompt: Would a Writer interface improve a permanently fixed single report?
question.answer: Not necessarily. The direct function is easier to read when there is no independent format choice.

opening.title: A policy edit can drift between formats
keyPoints: New requirement: high only above ten.
Plain output was updated.
Bracket output still applies the old boundary.
opening.narration: Imagine that an operations team changes the warning boundary from five to ten. In a combined implementation, each format has its own copy of the classification expression. A developer fixes the plain version but misses the bracket version. The two strings now disagree about the same observation even though both compile and run normally. Our demonstration uses the new requirement deliberately; the chapter's unchanged main example still uses five. This is the pressure that motivates a bridge. Put the classification decision in one report path, and let separate writers control punctuation. We need a boundary that prevents this kind of drift from spreading across combinations.
actions: Predict whether the two outputs agree before running.
Locate the duplicated business decision, not just duplicated punctuation.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch07.json → Locate the two decisions before drawing classes

question.prompt: Which concern was duplicated and then changed inconsistently?
question.answer: The warning classification threshold was duplicated in each formatting function.

opening.title: Separate meaning from punctuation
keyPoints: Report chooses a field name and validates data.
Writer formats the supplied field without changing meaning.
The stored Writer connection selects the pairing.
opening.narration: We can now name the design. Bridge keeps two related families connected through a stable operation so that they can grow independently. In this chapter, CountReport and WarningReport decide the meaning of the field. Plain and Brackets decide how that field is written. Report stores a borrowed Writer connection, and each concrete report crosses that connection during render. With two reports and two writers, we have four supported pairings but do not need four combination classes. This is not a promise that every imaginable display can use the same tiny operation. Independence only holds while the shared field contract carries the data each supported format needs.
actions: Point to the single classification expression in WarningReport.
Point to punctuation in each Writer implementation.
opening.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Locate the two decisions before drawing classes

question.prompt: Which side should change when brackets become braces?
question.answer: The formatting implementation should change; the report classification should remain the same.

mechanism.title: The abstraction role is not C++ syntax
keyPoints: Report is the high-level view offered to clients.
Writer is the lower-level formatting contract.
A Bridge can also use a concrete high-level class.
mechanism.narration: The traditional pattern word abstraction means the useful high-level view, not automatically an abstract C++ class. Here Report happens to be abstract because several report meanings need the same render operation. A single concrete report holding a Writer could still separate meaning from formatting. This distinction matters in reviews: counting abstract classes is not evidence that a bridge exists. Look instead for independently changing decisions connected through a useful operation. Writer::field receives a name and a number because these are the stable pieces of information both current formats can display. It should not ask which concrete report made the request.
actions: Ask whether one concrete CountReport plus two writers could still preserve the separation.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Locate the two decisions before drawing classes

question.prompt: Is an abstract C++ Report base required for every Bridge?
question.answer: No. The separation of independently varying responsibilities is central; an abstract high-level base depends on the actual caller needs.

theory.what: High-level reporting delegates formatting through a stable contract.
theory.where: Report holds writer_; concrete render methods call field.
theory.why: Meaning and appearance should change independently.
theory.invariant: Each writer preserves the supplied field meaning.
theory.risk: Type checks against concrete reports or writers recouple the families.

mechanism.title: Trace one value across the connection
keyPoints: CountReport validates six.
Writer receives the name count and value six.
Brackets returns [count:6] by value.
mechanism.narration: Follow cb.render with six. The selected object is a CountReport whose stored reference points to the Brackets object. CountReport first checks the domain rule, then calls writer_.field with count and six. The compiler checks that Writer offers this operation. Runtime virtual dispatch chooses the Brackets implementation. That implementation creates a new string and returns it through the report to the client. Data moves across the bridge as a field name and integer; control moves into the chosen writer and then back. No writer reference to the temporary name is saved. That makes the short call-time borrow safe under the current contract.
actions: Trace forward with arrows for calls, then backward with the returned string.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Trace data and control across the bridge

question.prompt: Where is the punctuation decision made for cb.render(6)?
question.answer: Inside Brackets::field, after CountReport validates the count and supplies the field name.

theory.what: A report call delegates formatting once and returns the resulting value.
theory.why: The report should not know bracket punctuation.
theory.invariant: The passed integer and name retain their meaning.
theory.risk: A writer that retains a reference to a temporary argument can later access dead storage.

mechanism.title: Two references, two lifetime duties
keyPoints: field borrows its name only during the call.
Report borrows its writer across many calls.
A reference member cannot be rebound.
mechanism.narration: The same ampersand can appear in two places with different practical obligations. The field parameter borrows a string only while that one function call is active. The writer_ member is stored in Report and may be used much later. Its source writer must therefore outlive all those report calls. In main, writers are constructed first, followed by reports, which gives the correct reverse destruction order. The reference also fixes the pairing during construction: assigning through a reference does not make it refer to another object. A runtime format switch would need a new report or a deliberately different connection design, with its own rules.
actions: Draw the short argument lifetime inside the longer report and writer lifetimes.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Trace data and control across the bridge

question.prompt: Can a setter rebind the existing const Writer& member?
question.answer: No. Construct a new report or redesign the connection as an explicitly managed pointer or owner if live switching is required.

theory.what: A report stores a non-owning connection selected at construction.
theory.why: Writers can be shared without copying their objects.
theory.invariant: The selected writer stays alive for each render call.
theory.risk: Returning a report that borrows a local writer creates a dangling connection.

mechanism.title: Syntax does not enforce semantic honesty
keyPoints: override catches a wrong virtual signature.
protected limits member access to the class family.
Tests still verify labels, thresholds, and formatting.
mechanism.narration: The compiler provides several useful checks, but none can read the business requirement. Protected makes writer_ and validate available to derived reports while keeping them out of ordinary client code. Static on validate means it uses no particular Report object's data. The conditional expression in WarningReport evaluates n greater than five and selects high or normal; its colon separates the two possible results. Override catches a mismatched field or render signature. However, a writer that changes six to seven still satisfies the type signature. Tests must verify that formatting preserves data and that the report chooses the correct label on both sides of the threshold.
actions: Explain the question mark and colon in the classification expression.
Ask which guarantees are checked by compilation and which need examples or tests.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → What compilation guarantees and what it cannot

question.prompt: Why test five and six rather than only a large count?
question.answer: They exercise the exact branch boundary: five is normal and six is high in the chapter contract.

theory.what: Language checks establish valid calls; tests establish required meaning.
theory.why: Independent components must share more than a matching signature.
theory.invariant: Every supported writer preserves the report-selected field and count.
theory.risk: Silent semantic changes compile successfully and can disagree across formats.

mechanism.title: Add CSV by extending one side
mechanism.eyebrow: MAINTENANCE / A TEST OF THE BOUNDARY
keyPoints: Add Csv::field without rewriting reports.
Test count, high, normal, and zero.
Fixed safe labels do not make a general CSV library.
mechanism.narration: The extension asks for comma-separated output. The useful test of our design is whether this format can be added without changing either report's decision logic. Csv implements field and joins the supplied name, a comma, and the number. That is sufficient for the existing fixed labels, because count, high, and normal contain no comma or quote. Do not claim that the result is a complete CSV encoder for arbitrary text. If labels become user-controlled, quoting and escaping become new requirements. A clear boundary makes that change local, but a boundary cannot eliminate the need to define the new format contract.
actions: Review the solution and verify that CountReport and WarningReport are unchanged.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → When the split helps, and when it does not

question.prompt: Why is name + comma + value sufficient only for this lab contract?
question.answer: The supported fixed names contain no CSV-special characters. Arbitrary names would need escaping and quoting rules.

comparisons.label: Runtime Writer
comparisons.text: Choose the format when constructing report objects.

comparisons.label: Template writer
comparisons.text: Choose a format type during compilation when that restriction fits.

comparisons.label: Enum plus function
comparisons.text: Keep a tiny fixed family in one simple formatting function.

closing.title: Independence has a price and a limit
keyPoints: Two types and four formats create eight combinations.
Separation reduces repeated implementation decisions.
A weak shared contract can force coupling back in.
closing.narration: Bridge is useful because the number of combinations grows as the product of the two choices. Two reports and four formats create eight possible pairings. Separate families can avoid writing a dedicated class for every pairing, but the combination behavior still needs thought and testing. If a new format requires information that field does not carry, forcing it into the interface may create special cases or concrete-type checks. That is evidence to revisit the contract. Sometimes an enum and a small switch is clearer for a closed set. The design is successful when real changes remain local, not when the diagram contains more boxes.
actions: Propose a format needing structured severity metadata and discuss whether the interface is sufficient.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → When the split helps, and when it does not

question.prompt: What warns that the two dimensions are no longer cleanly separated?
question.answer: Reports inspect concrete writer types, or writers inspect concrete report types to recover missing information.

closing.title: Bridge and Adapter can look alike
keyPoints: Bridge separates dimensions expected to vary.
Adapter repairs an existing interface mismatch.
A stored service connection alone proves neither pattern.
closing.narration: Both designs can show one object forwarding a call to another. That shared shape does not settle their purpose. In Adapter, a useful old service and an established caller disagree about an interface or meaning. In Bridge, we intentionally put reporting and formatting behind a connection so each side can develop independently. A real system can even place an adapter on one side of a bridge. The useful review question is therefore what change this boundary protects against. Here, adding a writer should not duplicate report policy. That story identifies Bridge more clearly than simply noticing a reference member.
actions: Ask learners to classify a vendor printer wrapper and then a report-format family.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → When the split helps, and when it does not

question.prompt: Can similar UML class shapes represent different patterns?
question.answer: Yes. Pattern intent, responsibilities, and the protected change boundary distinguish them.

closing.title: Defend a new report in plain language
keyPoints: Name the policy change.
State what Writer must receive.
Predict which existing tests remain unchanged.
closing.narration: Imagine adding a report that labels values above twenty as critical and others as routine. Before writing code, explain why the new labels belong to the report and why every current writer can still display them. Then ask whether the CSV contract remains safe with these fixed words. Existing CountReport and WarningReport tests should stay untouched because their rules have not changed. Add focused tests around twenty and twenty-one and test the new report with more than one writer. This exercise turns a memorized pattern into a maintenance plan: identify the changing responsibility, preserve the shared promise, and verify both the new decision and old behavior.
actions: Have learners give a one-minute change plan with one threshold test and one cross-format test.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Locate the two decisions before drawing classes

question.prompt: What is the smallest useful claim a Bridge test suite should support?
question.answer: Report policy stays consistent across supported writers, and each writer preserves the supplied field while applying its own format.
